The Five-bear rockling (Ciliata mustela) is a benthic teleost inhabiting coastal waters of the northeastern Atlantic, often found in rocky intertidal and subtidal zones. At a stable environmental temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], laboratory-maintained specimens have been observed to undergo yolk-sac resorption and transition to exogenous feeding within the first few days post-hatching. The modest size of this species is constrained by its habitat; maximum recorded lengths from field surveys on the Irish coast indicate that individuals rarely exceed 25.0 centimeters [Li = rarely exceed 25.0 centimeters], a value that aligns with the asymptotic size inferred from von Bertalanffy growth curves fitted to mark-recapture data. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, and the larval stage is brief. Egg diameter measurements, typically around 0.83 mm, were used to estimate a larval mass at birth of just 0.0003 grams [Wwb = 0.0003 grams], a figure that underscores the energetic vulnerability of these pelagic larvae prior to the onset of active feeding on copepod nauplii.

Recent growth studies under controlled conditions at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] have helped clarify the timing of reproductive development in Ciliata mustela. The attainment of sexual maturity, characterised by the first histological signs of active gametogenesis in the gonads, was recorded at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] in a laboratory cohort held at this stable temperature at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This single year of post-larval development is a relatively rapid maturation compared to larger-bodied gadiform relatives, which often require two or more years. There is notable sexual dimorphism in the length at which this pubertal transition occurs. Females typically undergo gonadal maturation upon reaching approximately 14.0 centimeters [Lp = approximately 14.0 centimeters] in total length, whereas males become reproductively active at a significantly smaller average dimension of 12.0 centimeters [Lp = 12.0 centimeters]. This divergence is likely linked to differing selective pressures on body size for gamete production versus territorial competition among males.

Reproductive output in this iteroparous species has been quantified through monitoring of captive spawning events. Gravid females produce demersal, adhesive eggs deposited in a single clutch per spawning event. The fecundity per event is substantial, with field estimates reporting approximately 30,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 30,000 eggs per clutch] for a fully mature female near the asymptotic length. The frequency of these reproductive events in the wild remains poorly documented, but laboratory observations at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] suggest that, under optimal thermal conditions, a gravid female can complete a full cycle of oocyte development and gamete release once per year [Ri = oocyte development and gamete release once per year]. These values collectively imply a substantial lifetime reproductive effort, though individual variation linked to maternal size and nutritional condition is considerable.

Longevity data for Ciliata mustela in the wild are sparse, but mark-recapture studies from the Wadden Sea, conducted at an ambient water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], indicate a maximal lifespan of approximately 1460 days [am = approximately 1460 days]. This corresponds to about four years, which is an intermediate duration among its intertidal fish associates; it is longer than that of many small blennioids but shorter than that of larger, deeper-dwelling gadids. The species appears to be an annual or short-lived perennial in terms of its reproductive window, with senescence and increased natural mortality observed in the fourth year. The 1460-day figure should be interpreted with caution, as it likely reflects the maximum under relatively stable, predator-moderated conditions rather than a universal species constant.

Comparative physiological studies reveal that the life-history strategy of the Five-bear rockling is finely tuned to cool temperate waters. The collection of measurements at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] is particularly relevant, as this temperature represents the approximate annual mean for their shallow-water habitat in the North Sea. At this temperature, the annual reproductive cycle appears tightly synchronised with spring plankton blooms, ensuring abundant prey for the pelagic larvae. The intermediate length at female puberty of 14.0 centimeters [Lp = 14.0 centimeters] falls between the values reported for the smaller, short-lived rockling species Gadus luscus and the larger, longer-lived Molva molva. This size-dependent fecundity means that a female reaching the maximum recorded total length can produce up to 30,000 eggs in a single seasonal spawning event [Ri = up to 30,000 eggs in a single seasonal spawning event], suggesting that the trade-off between early reproduction and attaining a larger adult body size is central to the species' life history.
